systems.name: Three-Region Harmonic Substitution System
systems.summary: The central system of the book organizes all chords into three functional regions — Root/Tonic (rest), Subdominant (distancing), and Dominant (tension) — and treats the II/V/I cadence as the master unit of harmonic motion. Within this framework, any chord may be replaced by another chord from the same harmonic region, and the dominant and subdominant regions are further declared interchangeable for the purpose of delay and color. The system is extended through tritone substitution (swap a dominant's root for its tritone), modal interchange (borrow chords from parallel modes sharing the same tonic), diminished symmetry (diminished chords repeat every minor third, yielding four equivalent options), and melodic minor dual membership (a minor II/V/I's half-diminished and altered dominant each belong to a different melodic minor key, unlocking additional substitutes). Turnaround progressions (II/V/I/VI and I/VI/II/V) and the all-dominant turnaround are structural extensions of the same cadential skeleton. The guitar-specific invariant throughout is that every concept must be internalized from both the 5th-string root position and the 6th-string root position.

members.name: Root Region (Tonic)
members.summary: Chords of rest: Cmaj7 (I), Em7 (IIIm), Am7 (VIm) in major; Cm7 (I), Ebmaj7 (bIII) in minor.

members.name: Subdominant Region
members.summary: Major subdominant: Fmaj7 (IV), Dm7 (IIm), Bbmaj7 (bVII). Minor subdominant: Fm7(6) (IVm), Bb7 (bVII), Abmaj7 (bVI), Dbmaj7 (bII).

members.name: Dominant Region
members.summary: Chords of tension: G7 (V) and Bø (VII); resolved by motion to tonic.

members.name: II/V/I Cadence
members.summary: The master organizational unit for chord progressions in both major and minor keys.

members.name: Turnaround Progression (II/V/I/VI or I/VI/II/V)
members.summary: II/V/I with an added VI degree; two structural forms, major and minor variants including VI7 and bVI7 options.

members.name: All-Dominant Turnaround
members.summary: Every chord in a turnaround progression made dominant with different voicings, each leading to the next until resolving to the tonic.

members.name: Tritone Substitution
members.summary: Replace a dominant 7th with another dominant 7th whose root is a tritone away; both share the same tritone interval.

members.name: Modal Interchange
members.summary: Borrowing chords from parallel modes (all modes sharing the same tonic) for re-harmonization color without abandoning the established key.

members.name: Diminished Chord Symmetry
members.summary: Diminished chords repeat every minor third, producing four equivalent chord options for any diminished symbol.

members.name: Fake Diminished
members.summary: An inverted dom7(b9) chord functioning as a dominant substitute.

members.name: Hybrid Diminished
members.summary: A diminished chord serving either as a connecting chord or as a V7 substitute in a cadence.

members.name: Melodic Minor Dual Membership
members.summary: In a minor II/V/I, the half-diminished chord is the VI of one melodic minor key and the altered dominant is the VII of another, unlocking two melodic minor substitution families.

members.name: Secondary Dominant
members.summary: A non-diatonic dominant chord assigned to resolve to a specific scale degree other than the tonic.

members.name: Lydian Dominant
members.summary: A dominant 7th chord that is neither the V degree nor a tritone substitution; tensioned with 9, 13, or #11.

traversal_rules.name: Same-Region Chord Interchangeability
traversal_rules.summary: Any chord may be replaced by another chord belonging to the same harmonic region; this is the theoretical basis for the IIm substituting for IV.

references.quote_excerpt: any chord of a given Harmonic Region may be replaced by another of the same region

traversal_rules.name: Subdominant-Dominant Interchangeability for Delay
traversal_rules.summary: Subdominant and dominant region chords are interchangeable; subdominant chords function to delay the dominant chord and add harmonic color.

references.quote_excerpt: subdominant chords are a way to delay the dominant chord, that is why subdominant chords and dominant chords are interchangeable

traversal_rules.name: Modal Interchange Column Traversal by Scale Degree
traversal_rules.summary: Each scale degree permits substitution only from specific columns of the modal interchange table, defining the allowed traversal paths between parallel-mode chords.

references.topic: Modal interchange substitution rules by degree
references.quote_excerpt: in every I degree we can use chords belonging from the 1st, 3rd or 6th columns

traversal_rules.name: Tritone Root Swap Traversal
traversal_rules.summary: Move from any dominant 7th to the dominant 7th whose root is a tritone away; both chords share the same tritone and are therefore functionally interchangeable.

references.quote_excerpt: replace a dominant 7th chord by another dominant 7th chord just by changing the bass of the chord with its tritone

traversal_rules.name: Diminished Chord Minor-Third Symmetry Traversal
traversal_rules.summary: Any diminished chord may be replaced by the diminished chord a minor third higher (or lower), cycling through four equivalent options.

references.quote_excerpt: Diminished Chords have an interesting characteristic, they repeat themselves every minor 3rd

traversal_rules.name: VII7 Leading-Tone Substitution for V7
traversal_rules.summary: The VII7 chord may substitute for V7 because all its notes are half-steps away from the notes of the tonic chord, creating strong voice-leading tension and resolution.

references.quote_excerpt: all the notes of B7 can work as leading tones to the notes of C6, because they are half step from each other

traversal_rules.name: All-Dominant Turnaround Chain Traversal
traversal_rules.summary: In a turnaround sequence, every chord is made dominant with varying voicings, each resolving to the next dominant until the final resolution to tonic.

references.quote_excerpt: all the chords of the turnaround become dominant with different voicings

traversal_rules.name: Dual Root-Position Learning (5th and 6th String)
traversal_rules.summary: Every voicing concept and cadence pattern must be internalized in both 5th-string and 6th-string root positions for complete fretboard coverage.

references.quote_excerpt: on the guitar we must learn things considering the 5th string as the root and also the 6th string as the root

modification_rules.name: Melody Governs Voicing Choice (Comping Constraint)
modification_rules.summary: When comping, the melody determines which voicing tensions and chord substitutions are available; improvising permits freer substitution choices.

references.quote_excerpt: the most important thing when comping is to follow the melody

modification_rules.name: Altered Tension Requirement on Minor-Key V7
modification_rules.summary: Dominant seventh chords functioning as V in a minor key almost always require altered tensions (b9, #9, #11, b13), distinguishing them from major-key dominant chords.

references.quote_excerpt: the dominant seventh chords almost always use altered tensions such as: b9, # 9, # 11, b13

modification_rules.name: Lydian Dominant Tension Rule (Non-Functional Dominants)
modification_rules.summary: Any dominant 7th that is not the V degree or a tritone substitution is treated as lydian dominant and tensioned with 9, 13, or #11.

references.quote_excerpt: Dominant 7th chords that are not the Vth degree or a tritone substitution, are always considered lydian dominant

modification_rules.name: Tritone Substitution Voicing Adjustment
modification_rules.summary: When a tritone substitute does not sound well with its original tension, both the tritone chord's extension and the preceding II chord's voicing must be adjusted together.

references.quote_excerpt: depending on the dominant chord we apply the tritone substitution to, it may not sound correct or great

modification_rules.name: Melodic Minor V-Degree Substitution Prohibition
modification_rules.summary: The V degree of a melodic minor scale may not substitute for the dominant chord in a cadence when it shares the same root as the tonic, as this obliterates the cadential function.

references.quote_excerpt: the melodic minor V degree chord might not work sometimes

modification_rules.name: Tensions Do Not Alter Cadential Function
modification_rules.summary: The tension notes (7, 9, 11, 13) added to any chord in a cadence do not change the cadence type or functional region of that chord.

references.quote_excerpt: the tension notes (7, 9, 11, 13) used over the chords below do not affect their function in any way

modification_rules.name: Parallel Mode Exercise Major-Key Anchor Rule
modification_rules.summary: In parallel-mode exercises, the first chord of any sequence must always be drawn from the major key; subsequent chords may be borrowed from the parallel minor.

references.quote_excerpt: the first chord of the sequence will always be from the major key

systems.name: Quartal Harmony Voicing System
systems.summary: A specialized voicing system built on stacked perfect fourths (and augmented/diminished fourths) that produces harmonically ambiguous 'hybrid' chords distinct from tertian harmony. The system's defining property is modal ambiguity: a single quartal voicing can represent multiple modes depending on which bass note is placed beneath it, making bass-note selection the primary traversal mechanism. Two architectural sub-techniques are named: Melodic Pedal Point (top voice held fixed while lower voices move) and Modal Quartal Chord Voicings (a quartal sequence adaptable across modes by changing the bass note). Voicing density and register are governed by explicit rules: 3rd-5th string roots are preferred over 6th-string roots to avoid muddiness, and tetrad voicings in low positions must be reduced to triads. The prescribed learning protocol is single-key immersion before transposing and selective memorization over exhaustive cataloguing.

members.name: Quartal Triad Voicing
members.summary: Three-note chord built from stacked fourths; preferred for lower register comping contexts.

members.name: Quartal Tetrad Voicing
members.summary: Four-note chord built from stacked fourths; must be reduced to triad when voiced too low or too densely.

members.name: Pentatonic Quartal Voicings
members.summary: Quartal voicings derived from major and relative minor pentatonic scales, excluding the avoid-note pentatonic.

members.name: Modal Quartal Chord Voicings
members.summary: Quartal chord sequences whose modal identity is determined by the sustained bass note beneath them.

members.name: Melodic Pedal Point (Quartal)
members.summary: A quartal voice-leading device where the top voice is held fixed while lower voices shift.

members.name: Polymodal Quartal Voicings
members.summary: Single quartal harmonic structures adaptable across multiple modes depending on bass note and context.

members.name: Minor Blues Scale Quartal Voicings
members.summary: Quartal shape (1, 4, b7) applied to harmonize the minor blues scale with scale notes always in the top voice.

traversal_rules.name: Bass Note Determines Modal Identity
traversal_rules.summary: Moving the sustained bass note beneath a fixed quartal chord sequence shifts the perceived mode of the entire sequence.

references.topic: Modal quartal voicing - bass note determines mode
references.quote_excerpt: if we play the bass note E continuously over the sequence of chords above, we would have a E Phrygian chord sequence

traversal_rules.name: Melodic Pedal Point: Fixed Top Voice with Moving Lower Voices
traversal_rules.summary: In melodic pedal point, the top voice remains stationary while lower quartal voices move, creating a distinct voice-leading texture.

references.quote_excerpt: Melodic pedal point is a concept where the lowest voicings of the chords move, but the top voice remains the same

traversal_rules.name: Locrian-as-Altered Substitution for Dominant Voicing
traversal_rules.summary: A dominant 7th altered chord's arpeggio is half-diminished, allowing it to be treated as Locrian and unlocking the entire major scale a half-step up as a quartal voicing source.

references.topic: Locrian vs. altered scale modal interchange
references.quote_excerpt: we can consider it for a while as being locrian, which allows us to use all the chords built from the major scale that generates it

traversal_rules.name: Pentatonic Scale Selection for Quartal Voicings over Major 7th
traversal_rules.summary: Over a major 7th chord, use G major pentatonic quartal voicings, C major pentatonic quartal voicings, or a mixture of both.

references.quote_excerpt: Over a Cmaj7 chord or any other chord belonging to the major scale

modification_rules.name: Comping Register Floor: 3rd-5th String Preference
modification_rules.summary: Quartal voicings for comping should start from the 3rd, 4th, or 5th strings; 6th-string-rooted voicings and low-position 5th-string voicings often produce undesirable muddiness.

references.topic: Comping register rule for quartal chords
references.quote_excerpt: we most often use the chords starting from the 3rd, 4th and 5th strings

modification_rules.name: Tetrad-to-Triad Density Reduction for Low Register
modification_rules.summary: When a quartal tetrad voicing sounds muddy due to low register or excessive density, drop the lowest note to produce a three-note quartal voicing.

references.quote_excerpt: some chords on the lower strings might not sound desirable, in these cases we can take out the lower note and play a 3 note quartal voicing

modification_rules.name: Lydian Dominant Voicing Restriction (Unresolved Dominant Only)
modification_rules.summary: Lydian dominant (mixolydian #4) quartal voicings may only be used over dominant 7th chords that are not resolving to another chord, except within a chain of successive dominant chords.

references.quote_excerpt: It can only be used over dominant 7th chords that are not leading to any other chord

modification_rules.name: Mixolydian Quartal Voicings Restricted to Major-Resolving V Chords
modification_rules.summary: Mixolydian quartal voicings on the V degree are only permissible when that V chord resolves to a major chord; they are excluded from minor cadence contexts.

references.topic: mixolydian voicings: major vs. minor cadence rule
references.quote_excerpt: mixolydian chord voicings, which can only be used when they are leading to major chords

modification_rules.name: Non-Family Chord Substitution When Voice-Leading Demands It
modification_rules.summary: A chord from outside the established voicing family may replace an expected chord when voice-leading logic produces a better result, as an explicit exception to family coherence.

references.quote_excerpt: sometimes can be replaced by a chord not belonging to that family

modification_rules.name: Minor Blues Scale Quartal: Scale Tones in Top Voice
modification_rules.summary: When harmonizing the minor blues scale with quartal shape (1, 4, b7), scale notes must always appear in the top voice of each chord; non-scale notes are permitted in inner voices.

references.topic: Minor blues scale quartal harmonization method
references.quote_excerpt: the scale notes will always be on the top voice of each chord

modification_rules.name: Locrian Voicing: Minor Blues Scale Replaces Minor Pentatonic
modification_rules.summary: Over Locrian quartal voicings, the minor pentatonic scale fails because its perfect 5th is not in the Locrian mode; the minor blues scale with #4 emphasis must substitute.

references.quote_excerpt: we must be careful when using the pentatonic scale over Locrian chord voicings, because the perfect 5th of the scale does not belong to this mode

systems.name: Open String Chord Voicing System
systems.summary: A guitar-specific voicing system that treats open strings as fixed pitches that constrain or color chord shapes. Chords are classified into two types: those locked to a specific key (non-transposable) and those that retain their shape but may shift quality when moved to different frets. The core discovery method is a two-step process: choose a chord shape retaining at least one open string, then systematically apply it across frets to identify viable voicings. Pedal point - a sustained bass or upper note while other voices move - is introduced as a baroque tension device organized into three practical string-based groups (6th string, 5th string, Drop D). The system prescribes short harmonic sequences (I/IVm, I/VI/IIm/V, etc.) as the primary deployment context, and mandates memorization of the foundational open-string chord vocabulary before advancing.

members.name: Key-Locked Open String Chords
members.summary: Chord shapes that can only be played in one key and cannot be transposed while retaining open strings.

members.name: Transposable Open String Chords
members.summary: Chord shapes that can be moved to other frets while retaining the same shape, though chord quality may shift.

members.name: Bass Pedal Point - 6th String (E)
members.summary: Chord sequences with the open 6th string sustained as a bass pedal tone.

members.name: Bass Pedal Point - 5th String (A)
members.summary: Chord sequences with the open 5th string sustained as a bass pedal tone.

members.name: Bass Pedal Point - Drop D
members.summary: Chord sequences using the 6th string retuned to D as the bass pedal; interchangeable with the 4th string D.

members.name: Inverted Pedal Point
members.summary: A sustained upper voice while lower voices move, creating top-voice pedal tension.

traversal_rules.name: Systematic Fret-Shifting Shape Discovery
traversal_rules.summary: After selecting an open-string chord shape, apply it to every fret in sequence to discover all viable voicings, most commonly using the 1st and 2nd open strings.

references.quote_excerpt: we can do some experimentation with all these chords by applying them on different frets of the guitar fretboard, leaving at least one open string

traversal_rules.name: Pedal Point Chord Short-Sequence Deployment
traversal_rules.summary: Pedal point and open string chords should be applied in simple, short harmonic sequences such as I/IVm, I/VI/IIm/V, IV/IVm/I, and I/V.

references.topic: How to use pedal point chords
references.quote_excerpt: The best way to use the pedal point chords or any open string chord, is to apply them as much as you can in every situation that is possible

modification_rules.name: Chord Quality Shift Warning When Moving Shapes
modification_rules.summary: Sliding a transposable open-string shape to a new fret can fundamentally change chord quality (e.g., major to minor); the player must verify the resulting quality at each fret.

references.topic: Chords that change identity by fret
references.quote_excerpt: some chords do not change their characteristics, but others can change completely, going from a major chord to a minor chord at times

modification_rules.name: Note Omission for Hand-Size Accommodation
modification_rules.summary: When an open-string chord shape is too difficult to fret, one or more notes may be omitted to make it playable without destroying the harmonic function.

references.quote_excerpt: depending on the size of our hand, some chords might be very difficult to play in determined keys
